To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the presence of bacteremia in very elderly patients (≥80 years of age) is associated with a 2-fold increase in mortality and that a high number of comorbidities, a low level of serum albumin, and a high number of antibiotics prescribed are the most relevant predictors of mortality.

the presence of bacteremia in patients aged 85 years and older is associated with a high mortality rate, and that a combination of the patient's functional status and the severity of infection can be used to predict mortality in these patients.

the most frequent cause of death among patients with bacteremia in a large, multicenter cohort of very elderly patients was sepsis, that the most frequent causes of sepsis were pneumonia, urinary tract infection, and skin infection, and that the most frequent pathogens were Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk of death from bacteremia in very elderly patients is higher than in younger adults, even in patients with a low severity of illness.
the elderly are not just a homogenous group of patients, but rather a heterogeneous group of patients with different needs and different outcomes.
